title: Reduced-gravity aircraft

{{Short description|Aircraft used to create brief weightlessness}}
[[File:Zero gravity flight trajectory C9-565 vector.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Trajectory for zero gravity maneuver]]
[[File:Mercury Astronauts in Weightless Flight on C-131 Aircraft - GPN-2002-000039.jpg|thumb|[[Project Mercury]] [[astronaut]]s on board a [[C-131 Samaritan]] flying as the "vomit comet" in 1959]]
[[File:KC-135 0G Aircraft Nicknamed Vomit Comet.jpg|thumb|KC-135 0-G aircraft nicknamed "Vomit Comet"]]
[[File:Physicist Stephen Hawking in Zero Gravity NASA.jpg|thumb|Physicist [[Stephen Hawking]] on board a reduced-gravity aircraft in April 2007]]

A '''reduced-gravity aircraft''' is a type of [[fixed-wing aircraft]] that provides brief near-weightless environments for training [[astronaut]]s, conducting research, and making gravity-free movie shots.

Versions of such airplanes were operated by the [[NASA]] Reduced Gravity Research Program,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/index.html |title=NASA Reduced Gravity Research Program |publisher=Jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov |date=2009-03-17 |access-date=2009-09-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090825085742/http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/index.html |archive-date=2009-08-25 }}</ref> and one is currently operated by the Human Spaceflight and Robotic Exploration Programmes of the European Space Agency. The unofficial nickname "'''vomit comet'''" became popular among those who experienced their operation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/audience/forstudents/brainbites/nonflash/bb_home_vomitcomet.html|title=NASA - What's the Vomit Comet?|access-date=May 15, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120505001314/http://www.nasa.gov/audience/forstudents/brainbites/nonflash/bb_home_vomitcomet.html|archive-date=May 5, 2012}}</ref>

== History ==

Parabolic flight as a way of simulating weightlessness was first proposed by the German aerospace engineer Fritz Haber and his brother, physicist [[Heinz Haber]] in 1950.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Haber | first1=Fritz | last2=Haber | first2=Heinz | title=Possible methods of producing the gravity-free state for medical research| journal= Journal of Aviation Medicine | date=1950| volume=21 | issue=5 | pmid=14778792 | pages=395–400}} Summary of the article: {{Cite journal|last1=Campbell|first1=Mark R.|doi=10.3357/ASEM.26010.2009|pmid=20027862|title=Classics in space medicine. Possible methods of producing the gravity-free state for medical research|journal=Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine|volume= 80 |issue= 12|year=2009|page=1077}}</ref> Both had been brought to the US after [[World War II]] as part of [[Operation Paperclip]].<ref>{{Cite news|first1=Ford|last1=Burkhard|title=Fritz Haber, 86, Dies; Simulated Weightlessness of Space|journal=New York Times|date=1998-08-28|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/08/29/us/fritz-haber-86-dies-simulated-weightlessness-of-space.html}}</ref> As well, [[Shih-Chun Wang]] studied nausea in astronauts for [[NASA]], which helped lead to the creation of the vomit comet.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.news-gazette.com/news/new-chancellor-took-her-own-path/article_83ee0f63-96a4-5ae5-85b1-61595156d4c0.html |title=New chancellor took her own path | News |publisher=news-gazette.com |date=2011-10-16 |access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

Parabolic flights are sometimes used to examine the effects of weightlessness on a living organism. While humans are by far the most common passengers, animals have occasionally been involved in experiments, including a notable experiment on how weightlessness affected a [[domestic cat]]'s [[Cat righting reflex|righting reflex]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O9XtK6R1QAk |title=Weightless Cats - Do Space Cats Land On Their Feet? |publisher=YouTube |date=2011-01-11 |access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref> and a [[pigeon]]'s attempts to navigate in a weightless state.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4sZ3qe6PiI |title=Pigeons In Space |publisher=YouTube |date=2011-02-04 |access-date=2020-02-16}}</ref>

== Operating principles ==
The aircraft gives its occupants the sensation of weightlessness by following a [[parabola|parabolic]] flight path, which is the path that objects naturally follow while in [[free fall]].<ref>William Tyrrell Thomson, Introduction to Space Dynamics, Dover 1986. p. 91.</ref> The aircraft is used in this way to demonstrate to astronauts what it is like to [[orbit]] the Earth. 
During this time the aircraft does not need to exert any [[ground reaction force]] on its contents to keep them stationary relative to the aircraft, causing the sensation of weightlessness.

Initially, the aircraft climbs with a pitch angle of about 45 degrees. The sensation of weightlessness is achieved by reducing thrust and lowering the nose to maintain a neutral, or "zero lift", configuration such that the aircraft follows the same path that an object in free fall, with no air resistance, would follow. Engine thrust is used to exactly compensate for drag. Weightlessness begins at the point when the plane starts to follow this parabolic path, which is while the plane is ascending. It lasts through the rest of the ascent, and into the descent phase, until the aircraft must pull up, usually when it reaches a downward pitch angle of around 30 degrees. The aircraft then pulls back up to repeat the maneuver. During this pull-up, the forces felt are roughly twice that of gravity. This cycle can be repeated.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/trajectory.html |title=C-9B Flight Trajectory |publisher=Jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov |date=2009-03-17 |access-date=2009-09-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091213132109/http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/trajectory.html |archive-date=2009-12-13 }}</ref>

This aircraft is used to train astronauts in zero-g maneuvers, giving them about 25 seconds of weightlessness out of 65 seconds of flight in each [[parabola]]. During such training, the airplane typically flies about 40–60 parabolic manoeuvres. In about two thirds of the passengers, these flights produce [[nausea]] due to [[airsickness]],<ref name=SpaceInterviewYaniec>{{cite web |url=http://www.space.com/peopleinterviews/yaniec_991020.html |title=Flying The Vomit Comet Has Its Ups And Downs |publisher=space.com |date=October 20, 1999 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060310204522/http://www.space.com/peopleinterviews/yaniec_991020.html |archive-date=2006-03-10 |last=Golightly |first=Glen}}</ref><ref name=PhysicsCentral>{{cite web
| url = http://www.physicscentral.com/explore/einstein/wyp2005/projects/freefall/051006.cfm
| title = Reduced Gravity: Vomit Comet Blog 
| access-date = 2007-11-07
|date= May 10, 2005
| work = PhysicsCentral
}}</ref> giving the plane its nickname "vomit comet".

==Operators==

===Canada===
The [[Canadian Space Agency]] and the [[National Research Council (Canada)|National Research Council]] have a [[Falcon 20]] used for microgravity research.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/eng/facilities/iar/falcon.html|title=Falcon 20 - Facilities - NRC-CNRC|access-date=June 26, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611195513/http://www.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/eng/facilities/iar/falcon.html|archive-date=June 11, 2011}}</ref> The small plane is normally not used for people to float freely and experience weightlessness; however, comedian [[Rick Mercer]] did so for a segment of his [[Rick Mercer Report|show]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k3xSYRa9G0g |title=RMR: Rick and Zero Gravity |publisher=YouTube |date=2011-06-16 |access-date=2016-02-24}}</ref>

===Ecuador===
[[Image:Exa-fae-05-1.jpg|thumb|200px|Ecuadorian crew in weightlessness]]
The first zero G plane to enter service in Latin America is a [[North American Sabreliner|T-39 Sabreliner]] nicknamed ''CONDOR'', operated for the [[Ecuadorian Civilian Space Agency]] and the [[Ecuadorian Air Force]] since May 2008.<ref name="EXA 2008-05-06">{{cite web|url=http://exa.ec/bp16/index-en.html |title=Exa And Fae Develops First Zero-G Plane In Latin America |publisher=Exa.ec |date=2008-04-10 |access-date=2009-09-14}}</ref> On June 19, 2008, this plane carried a seven-year-old boy, setting the Guinness world record for the youngest person to fly in microgravity.<ref name="Guinness">{{cite web|url=https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/adjudications/080623_Youngest_Person_Microgravity.aspx |title=Youngest person to experience microgravity |publisher=Guinnessworldrecords.com |access-date=2009-09-14}}</ref>

===Europe===
Since 1984, [[European Space Agency|ESA]] and the [[CNES]] have flown reduced-gravity missions in a variety of aircraft, including NASA's KC-135, a [[Sud Aviation Caravelle|Caravelle]], an [[Ilyushin Il-76MDK]], and an [[Airbus A300]] known as the ''Zero-G''. In 2014 the A300 was phased out in favor of a more modern [[Airbus A310]], also named ''Zero-G''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.airzerog.com/en/who-we-are/novespace.html |title=Air Zero-G About Us |publisher=airzerog.com |access-date=2014-03-11}}</ref> It is based at [[Aéroport de Bordeaux Mérignac|Bordeaux-Mérignac airport]] in [[France]], operated by Novespace, and has also been flown from [[Paris–Le Bourget Airport|Paris Le Bourget airport]] and [[Dübendorf Air Base]] in Switzerland.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spaceflight.esa.int/users/index.cfm?act=default.page&level=11&page=paraf |title=ESA's A300 Zero-G Program |language=nl |publisher=Spaceflight.esa.int |access-date=2009-09-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090828010421/http://www.spaceflight.esa.int/users/index.cfm?act=default.page&level=11&page=paraf |archive-date=2009-08-28 }}</ref> Since 1997 CNES subsidiary Novespace has handled the management of these flights.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cnes.fr/web/CNES-en/3014-pr56-2004-new-parabolic-flight-campaign.php|title=CNES: PR56-2004 - New parabolic flight campaign|access-date=October 4, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090627032808/http://www.cnes.fr/web/CNES-en/3014-pr56-2004-new-parabolic-flight-campaign.php|archive-date=June 27, 2009}}</ref>

This {{illm|Airbus A310 Zero G|lt=A310 Zero G|fr|Airbus A310 Zero G}} aircraft is used also to realize commercial flights for public passengers in partnership between operator Novespace and the {{ill|Avico|fr}} company, under Air Zero G brand.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aircosmosinternational.com/french-astronaut-performs-moonwalk-on-parabolic-flight-84817|title=French astronaut performs "Moonwalk" on parabolic flight - Air & Cosmos - International|work=Air & Cosmos - International|access-date=2017-08-29|language=en}}</ref> The aircraft has also been used for cinema purposes, with [[Tom Cruise]] and [[Annabelle Wallis]] filming for ''[[The Mummy (2017 film)|The Mummy]]'' in 2017.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/behind-screen/mummy-behind-scenes-zero-g-stunt-1011921|title='The Mummy': Behind the Scenes of That Zero-G Stunt (Exclusive)|work=The Hollywood Reporter|access-date=2017-08-29|language=en}}</ref>

===Russia===
In Russia, commercial flights are offered on the [[Ilyushin Il-76MDK]] jet; several U.S. companies book flights on these jets.<ref name="BoyleCBS">{{cite web |first=Alan |last=Boyle |url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/5992077 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140829090517/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/5992077/ |archive-date=August 29, 2014 |title=Zero-gravity flights go mainstream |publisher=NBC News |date=2004-09-16 |access-date=2009-09-14}}</ref>

The [[Indian Air Force|Indian Air force]] also used them to train the first batch of Indian Astronauts for the [[Indian Human Spaceflight Programme|Gaganyaan Project]] of [[ISRO]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sharma |first=Ritu |date=2024-03-04 |title=From Fighter Pilots To Astronauts – How IL-76 Aircraft Helped India Train Its 'Vyomnauts' For 1st Manned Space Mission |url=https://www.eurasiantimes.com/from-fighter-pilots-to-astronauts-how-il-76-aircraft/ |access-date=2024-05-21 |website=Latest Asian, Middle-East, EurAsian, Indian News |language=en-US}}</ref>

===United States===
[[Image:PeterZG-small.jpg|thumb|right|upright|[[Peter Diamandis]] of [[Zero Gravity Corporation]]]]

====NASA====
[[Image:A300 Zero G.jpg|thumb|A300-Zero-G]]

NASA flew zero gravity flights on various aircraft for many years. In 1959 [[Project Mercury]] astronauts trained in a [[C-131 Samaritan]] aircraft dubbed the "vomit comet".<ref name="NASA 2002">{{cite web|url=http://nix.larc.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=GPN-2002-000039|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150214204039/http://nix.larc.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=GPN-2002-000039|archive-date=2015-02-14|title=Mercury Astronauts in Weightless Flight on C-131 Aircraft|date=2006-08-02|access-date=2013-05-14}}. Page hosts a NASA photograph dated 01/01/1959<!-- this image is also at [[Image:Mercury Astronauts in Weightless Flight on C-131 Aircraft - GPN-2002-000039.jpg]]-->.</ref>

Twin [[KC-135 Stratotanker]]s were used until December 2004 and later retired. One, a KC-135A registered N930NA (also known as NASA 930, formerly USAF serial no. 59-1481), flew more than 58,000 parabolas after NASA acquired it in 1973, before being retired in 1995. It is now on display at [[Ellington Field]], near the [[Johnson Space Center]]. The other (N931NA or NASA 931, formerly AF serial no. 63-7998) was also used by [[Universal Pictures]] and [[Imagine Entertainment]] for filming scenes involving weightlessness in the movie ''[[Apollo 13 (film)|Apollo 13]]''; it made its final flight on October 29, 2004, and is permanently stored in the [[Pima Air & Space Museum]] in Tucson, Arizona.

In 2005 NASA replaced these aircraft with a [[McDonnell Douglas]] [[McDonnell Douglas C-9|C-9B Skytrain II]] (N932NA) formerly owned by [[KLM|KLM Royal Dutch Airlines]] and the [[United States Navy]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/C_9B_history.html |title=C-9B History |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=2009-09-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091215054816/http://jsc-aircraft-ops.jsc.nasa.gov/Reduced_Gravity/C_9B_history.html |archive-date=2009-12-15 }}</ref>

NASA concluded the Reduced Gravity Research Program and ended operations in July 2014, due to aircraft technical problems. It is replaced with private company contracts.

{{As of|2015}} NASA had a microgravity services contract with [[Zero Gravity Corporation]] (ZERO-G) and used its aircraft, G-FORCE ONE, a modified Boeing [[727-200]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://flightopportunities.nasa.gov |title=Flight Opportunities program |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=2013-04-22}}</ref>

====Other operators====
In late 2004, the [[Zero Gravity Corporation]] became the first company in the United States to offer zero-g flights to the general public, using [[Boeing 727]] jets. Each flight consists of around 15 parabolas, including simulations of the gravity levels of the Moon and Mars, as well as complete weightlessness.<ref name="BoyleCBS"/>

In 2015, [[Integrated Spaceflight Services]], began serving as the research and education integrator of the [[National Research Council of Canada]] for the US market, offering comprehensive reduced-gravity services on a modified [[Falcon 20]] aircraft.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.integratedspaceflight.com/our-services/reduced-gravity-services/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141212080155/http://www.integratedspaceflight.com/our-services/reduced-gravity-services/|archive-date=December 12, 2014|title=Integrated Spaceflight Services|website=Integratedspaceflight.com|access-date=2015-04-06}}</ref> ISS has flown annual microgravity research campaigns to evaluate space suits and other technologies with [[Project PoSSUM]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.space.com/38832-spacesuit-zero-g-testing-canadian-flight.html|title=Private Spacesuit Undergoes Zero-G Testing to Prepare for Commercial Flight|date=2017-11-20|access-date=2020-08-07|language=en}}</ref>

[[Aurora Aerospace]] in [[Oldsmar, Florida]] offers zero-g flights using a [[Fuji/Rockwell Commander 700]]. It is also used to simulate the gravity of the Moon and Mars.<ref>{{cite web |title=Our Training Programs |url=http://www.aurora-aerospace.com/index.php/training-programs/ |work=Aurora Aerospace |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090130024613/http://www.aurora-aerospace.com/index.php/training-programs |archive-date=2009-01-30 }}</ref>

==Airsickness==
According to former Reduced Gravity Research Program director John Yaniec, anxiety contributes most to passengers' airsickness. The stress on their bodies creates a sense of panic and therefore causes the passenger to vomit. Yaniec gives a rough estimate of passengers, that "one third <nowiki>[become]</nowiki> violently ill, the next third moderately ill, and the final third not at all." Vomiting is referred to as being "ill".<ref name=SpaceInterviewYaniec />

[[Hyoscine hydrobromide|Scopolamine]] is often used as an [[antiemetic]] during reduced-gravity-aircraft training.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Reduced-gravity Environment Hardware Demonstrations of a Prototype Miniaturized Flow Cytometer and Companion Microfluidic Mixing Technology | pmc=4354048 | pmid=25490614 | doi=10.3791/51743 | issue=93 | year=2014 | journal=J Vis Exp | article-number=e51743 | last1 = Phipps | first1 = WS | last2 = Yin | first2 = Z | last3 = Bae | first3 = C | last4 = Sharpe | first4 = JZ | last5 = Bishara | first5 = AM | last6 = Nelson | first6 = ES | last7 = Weaver | first7 = AS | last8 = Brown | first8 = D | last9 = McKay | first9 = TL | last10 = Griffin | first10 = D | last11 = Chan | first11 = EY}}</ref>

== Use in media production ==
The 1995 film ''[[Apollo 13 (film)|Apollo 13]]'' filmed many scenes aboard NASA's KC-135 parabolic aircraft.

In 2016, rock group [[OK Go]] recorded a music video for their single "[[Upside Down & Inside Out]]" on a reduced-gravity aircraft, which involved acrobatic choreography created specifically for the zero-gravity environment.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Allain|first=Rhett|date=February 12, 2016|title=The Physics of OK Go's Epic New Zero-G Video|language=en-US|work=[[Wired (website)|Wired]]|url=https://www.wired.com/2016/02/the-physics-of-ok-gos-epic-new-zero-g-video/|access-date=2021-07-23|issn=1059-1028}}</ref>

The adult entertainment production company [[Private Media Group]] has filmed a [[pornography|pornographic]] movie called ''[[The Uranus Experiment|The Uranus Experiment: Part Two]]'' where a zero-gravity intercourse scene was filmed aboard a reduced-gravity aircraft. The filming process was particularly difficult from a technical and logistical standpoint. Budget constraints allowed for only one {{nowrap|20-second}} shot, featuring the actors [[Sylvia Saint]] and Nick Lang.<ref name="aw">{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000620033738/http://www.space.com/sciencefiction/movies/uranus_experiment_000516.html |title=Zero Gravity Sex Film Up for Award |date=16 May 2000 |url=http://www.space.com/sciencefiction/movies/uranus_experiment_000516.html |website=SPACE.com |access-date=25 January 2014 |archive-date=20 June 2000}}</ref> [[Berth Milton, Jr.|Berth Milton, Jr]]<!-- president at 2000 -->, president and [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] of Private Media Group, said in 2000 "You would not want to be afraid of flying, that's for sure!"<ref name="in">{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706183639/http://www.space.com/sciencefiction/movies/milton_interview_000516.html |title='To Boldly Go': Star Trek, Sex and Space |date=16 May 2000 |website=SPACE.com |url=http://www.space.com/sciencefiction/movies/milton_interview_000516.html |archive-date=6 July 2008}}</ref>
 
The ZERO-G corporation was featured in the ''[[MythBusters]]'' [[MythBusters (2008 season)#Episode 104 – "NASA Moon Landing"|NASA Moon Landing Conspiracy episode]], in which it flew [[Adam Savage]] and [[Jamie Hyneman]] on a custom flight path to replicate the Moon's gravity. This allowed Savage to replicate the footage of [[Neil Armstrong]] walking on the Moon, disarming [[Moon landing conspiracy theories|claims that the footage was forged]].
